Digital technology hasn't fixed every single problem we have with photography. This is a very easy thing to explain, and I'm just an amateur photographer; there are several things you have to take into account to get an intelligible photo. One of these is the speed of the shutter (non-digital technology, here folks)- which is the amount of time it is actually open in an analog camera. In a digital camera it is the length of time the digital sensor is exposed to light.

The next thing is the opening of the aperture called the F Stop- even digital cameras will work this way. It is how wide the lens is, to put it really simple, is how much light it will let in at one time. The F stop can influence the focal length- how much of the subject you are taking a picture of- is in sharp focus or not.

So when we combine these elements in the right proportions, we can get a good picture- plenty of light, a sensitive film (or sensor), and a sharp focus on the subject. The problem come when you are not shooting pictures in ideal conditions, and space is far from ideal! The expanse is very dark, except for the stars, and punctuated in our solar system by the sun and the planets that reflect the sunlight.

Yes, our eyes are awesome creations, we can see dim things and bright things. A camera cannot; it sees the world in a shades of gray, and cannot adjust the way our eyes do when we are looking at a picture of something super bright AND dark at the same time. This is essentially what is going on in this picture; the moon is super bright, and space (including the stars) is super dark. The stars are really dim, but our eyes can make up for that and lets us see really bright and really dim things in one picture.

The moon reflects the sun's rays with incredible efficiency, the dust on the surface is composed not only of carbon black, but also silicates (which is powdered glass- think of a mirror). So this incredibly bright celestial object (the moon) to the camera is photographed by having a short shutter speed and a high sensitivity to light, not letting the dim stars get bright enough in the picture for us to see. If we slowed down the shutter speed and let light in for a longer time, the moon would be so bright it would lose any sharp focus or distinction, but we would finally see the stars behind it.

This is what happens when we let our digital gadgets do our thinking for us; we loose the basic understanding of how they work and the job they do.
